cells.tense: Right now the structure is already set and someone else's feeling moves through it
cells.ask: Name one thing you do each week to hold the room together, and tell one person what it costs you.
cells.core:
You know how to hold someone's feeling without picking it up and carrying it away. That's harder than it sounds, and it means people tell you things they don't tell other people.

The structure around you is holding, and you're the one keeping it that way — not by controlling it, by staying steady in it. That steadiness is doing more than you probably say out loud. When someone comes apart near you, they don't fall very far, because you've already made the shape that catches them. That's the thing people lean on without naming. You made a container wide enough for what comes and strong enough to stay standing.

cells.tense: Somewhere up ahead someone will need the room to already be ready and right
cells.ask: Leave one arrangement alone this week, and watch what happens when you do not tend it.
cells.core:
You're already braced for a feeling that hasn't arrived. Before anyone asks, you've built the room around them — predicted the mood, laid out the response, decided what they'll need by Thursday. It looks like care. Some of it is care.

But you're spending real energy on a moment you can't actually see yet, and the people you're doing it for can feel the push. Holding someone and steering them look similar from the outside. From the inside, one lets them breathe. The readiness is crowding out the room it was meant to make. The support is there. The person might not get to reach for it.

cells.tense: The room went quiet a while back and you're still standing where the sound stopped
cells.ask: Say one true thing about how you feel to one person this week, before you decide what it means.
cells.core:
The structure holds, but it doesn't reach. You can set the frame — the hours, the order, the way things get done — and stay out of what moves through it. On a bad night the useful thing is close to hand and the near thing isn't. It might not be refusing anyone. It might just be that the frame became the whole job.

People want the part of you that doesn't have a plan. Saying one true thing before you've worked out what it means shifts the whole room, and it tends to land. That honesty is the real frame anyway, holding through what you actually say rather than the shape you keep around it. Say the true thing once. Let it be yours.

cells.tense: The room is already responding to the shape you're keeping, whether or not you call it yours
cells.ask: Tell one person what you were actually doing when you got quiet — you organized the room so they could be heard.
cells.core:
You're shaping how people feel around you — the pace, the tone, whether it's safe to say the hard thing — and you talk about it like it just happens. You move a conversation, place a silence, keep bad news from landing on the person who's already tired.

None of that is accidental, and none of it is on anyone else. Naming it would hold better. Not as a boast, as a fact — this is something you do, and something you can decide when to stop doing. The choice has been yours the whole time. It just hasn't had your name on it yet.
